## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and catalog data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Ruhakajātaka* (Ja 191) is a narrative in the Pali *Jātaka* collection. In the frame narrative set at Jetavana, the Buddha recounts the story for the sake of a monk tempted by his former wife, an occasion cross-referenced to the Indriya Jātaka of the Aṭṭhakanipāta [Fausböll 1879]. In the story of the past, the Bodhisatta is King Brahmadatta of Bārāṇasī, and Ruhaka is his royal chaplain (*purohita*) [Appleton 2010; Fausböll 1879]. When Ruhaka becomes estranged from his wife following an incident that caused him public humiliation, the king summons him and attempts to reconcile the couple, uttering a stanza that compares their reconciliation to repairing a broken bowstring [Appleton 2010; Fausböll 1879]. Ruhaka, however, rejects the king's advice, replying in verse that so long as hemp and craftsmen are available a new bowstring can be fashioned, and subsequently takes a new wife [Appleton 2010; Fausböll 1879]. In the story's resolution (*samodhāna*), the Bodhisatta is identified with the king, the dissatisfied monk with Ruhaka, and the former wife with Ruhaka's estranged wife [Fausböll 1879].

  Computational analysis by DharmaNexus registers five internal text-reuse segments shared with the second volume of the *Jātaka-aṭṭhakathā* (longest match §1.3–2.4 to §706–710), with no cross-language alignments meeting the score threshold [DharmaNexus].
